summary: Two fractions are equivalent when they mark the SAME point (same magnitude) on a number line or the same length on a strip, even though they are written with different numerators and denominators. Families such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 arise because re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts leaves the position unchanged. Stacked/aligned 0–1 number lines, dual labels above and below one line, and length-matched fraction strips make the coincident points visible. The documented hard cases are (a) accepting two differently-written fractions as the same point and (b) finding an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. locating 1/2 as 3/6 on a line divided into sixths). Re-partitioning only produces a new name when the finer parts subdivide evenly all the way to the point.
misconceptions: Cannot accept two differently-written fractions as the same point (IES Roadblock 2.3)
Cannot locate an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. finding 1/2 as 3/6 on a sixths line)
'Different numbers can't name the same amount' — denies equivalence altogether
Additive drift — thinks 1/2 and 2/3 are equivalent because you 'add 1 to each'
Whole-number bias — 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are larger

activities.title: Plumb-line on stacked thirds and sixths lines
steps: Stack a 0–1 line divided into thirds directly above a 0–1 line divided into sixths, carefully aligned at 0 and 1.
Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and drop a vertical plumb-line straight down to the sixths line.
Name the fraction on the sixths line that sits at exactly the same point (4/6), and state in words: two different names, one position.
Repeat for other target points and record each equivalent pair you find.
Say aloud why the shared point means the two fractions are equal in size.
activities.insight: Equivalent fractions are different names for the SAME point on the number line; same position means same magnitude.

activities.title: Re-partition toggle: the point that does not move
steps: Start on a thirds line with 2/3 marked.
Split each third into two equal parts to create a sixths line, keeping the 0–1 ends fixed.
Observe whether the 2/3 mark moves, and add the new label 4/6 to that same point.
Explain in your own words why subdividing each part does not shift the position, only adds a finer-grained name.
Now locate 1/2 on a line divided into sixths by splitting each half into three (not two): count three sixths to the midpoint and mark 3/6 at the 1/2 point.
activities.insight: Re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts preserves a fraction's position, which is why equivalent families exist. When the finer partition subdivides evenly all the way to the point, that same point simply gains a new name (1/2 becomes 3/6 on a sixths line); when the partition does not reach the point (e.g. fifths for 1/2), no such name exists.

activities.title: Measuring equal lengths with different fraction strips
steps: Lay a 1/2 strip, a 2/4 strip and a 3/6 strip along the same 0–1 length.
Check by eye and by measuring that they reach the same endpoint (allowing for the slight thickness and cutting error of physical strips).
State that 'same length = same number' even though the pieces and labels differ.
Find and record at least three fractions equal to 1/2 using the strips and/or a number line (e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10).
activities.insight: Equivalence can also be felt as equal length: differently-partitioned strips that reach the same point name the same amount.

activities.title: Contrast renaming with 'add one to each'
steps: On a shared 0–1 line with 2/3 marked, predict where 3/4 (from 'add 1 to top and bottom') would land.
Place 3/4 on the line and observe it sits to the RIGHT of 2/3, at a different point.
Compare this +1 shift with splitting each part into finer pieces, which did not move the mark.
Explain why adding the same number to numerator and denominator is NOT the same as finding an equivalent.
activities.insight: Equivalence is a shared point produced by re-partitioning; adding the same amount to numerator and denominator is not a valid way to find equivalents, because for any fraction other than one whole it moves the point (2/3 -> 3/4 is further right), so the new fraction is not equivalent. (The only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 -> 3/3, which stays at 1.)

activities.title: Verify and sort equivalents (practice and check)
steps: Decide for pairs such as 'do 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point?' and justify using a line or strip.
Match equivalent fractions to a target fraction.
Sequence a set of fractions in order along a number line.
Sort cards into 'equivalent to 1/2' and 'not equivalent to 1/2', explaining each placement.
activities.insight: Once the same-point idea is built, learners can reliably verify, match and sort equivalents and justify their decisions by position or length.

checkQuestion: Show stacked 0-to-1 number lines, one divided into thirds and one into sixths, lined up. Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and ask: 'Which fraction on the sixths line is at exactly the same point, and how do you know they are equal?' Then ask: 'Show me on these lines three fractions that are all equal to 1/2.'
checkAnswer: 4/6 is at the same point as 2/3 — same position means same magnitude, so 2/3 = 4/6 (each third splits into two sixths, the point does not move). Three fractions equal to 1/2: e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10, each marking the midpoint of 0–1.
